entries.label: Variation
entries.general: Differences among the members of a set, such as organisms, practices, designs or candidate solutions. These differences give selection and chance something to act on. Variation matters for change over time only when some of it is passed on.

facets.biology: Individuals of a species differ in the versions of genes they carry (alleles) and in the traits these help produce. New versions arise by mutation, and recombination shuffles existing ones. Only differences that parents pass on count toward evolution.
facets.culture: People differ in the words, skills and beliefs they hold. Differences arise from invention and from copying errors, and only those that others learn can spread. Pottery styles and first names are tracked this way.
facets.technology: Versions of a tool, machine or program differ in materials, shape and code. They arise from deliberate changes and from imperfect copying of an earlier design. Only versions that are built or recorded can be copied later.
facets.AI and computation: The candidates in an evolutionary algorithm differ in their encoded contents. Random mutation and crossover (mixing two parents) create new differences. If the pool loses its variety, the search stalls.

entries.excludes: Variation builds up only if it is passed on, by genes in biology and by learning or copying elsewhere. A tan is not inherited. Cultural and computing variants can be made on purpose, while mutation ignores need. Diversity of kinds, such as many species, is a different idea.

entries.label: Evolutionary Process
entries.general: Change in the make-up of a population of variants over repeated rounds of copying or reproduction. Variants arise, are passed on, and differ in how often they are kept, by selection and by chance. Rounds are generations, turns of social learning or algorithm cycles.

facets.biology: Populations of organisms change across generations in the heritable traits they carry. Mutation and recombination supply variants. Selection, chance and isolation change which variants are common.
facets.culture: Practices, words and designs held by a community change as people learn from one another. Invention and copying errors supply variants. Biased adoption, chance and group size change which variants are common.
facets.technology: Designs change across successive versions. Makers vary a design, buyers and testers favor some versions, and later makers copy those. Parts can also be borrowed from unrelated designs.
facets.AI and computation: An evolutionary algorithm keeps a pool of candidate solutions. Each round it varies candidates, scores them and copies higher scorers into the next round. The programmer sets the pool, the scoring rule and the number of rounds.

entries.excludes: One growing organism or one tuned program is not a population evolving. Biological variants arise without regard to need, and evolution has no target. An evolutionary algorithm has one, set by its programmer. Trial and error in one person as selection (Skinner, Campbell) is contested and left out.

entries.label: Niche Construction
entries.general: Organisms or groups change their surroundings, and the changes alter the conditions that later members of their own or other populations face. The changes often outlast the individuals who made them. They may be accidental or planned.

facets.biology: Beavers build dams, earthworms change soil and termites build mounds. The changes last, so descendants and neighbors face altered conditions and different traits may do well. No plan is needed.
facets.culture: Farming, herding, building and fire use change landscapes, diets and disease. Later generations inherit the altered conditions together with the knowledge. Dairy farming raised the advantage of genes that let adults digest milk sugar.

entries.excludes: Intent is optional: dams and earthworm soil are unplanned, while farming is often planned. A change counts only if it alters later conditions for the maker or others. Footprints that the next tide erases do not. It changes what selection acts on and carries no plan for evolving.

entries.label: Domestication
entries.general: A long-running two-way relationship in which people shape another species' breeding and that species shapes human food, work and settlement. It is a case of niche construction and coevolution.

facets.biology: People choose which plants or animals breed and supply food and shelter. Over generations the kept population shifts, as in tamer animals or seed-holding plants. Some selection is deliberate and some is an unplanned effect of life with people.
facets.culture: Keeping crops and herds changes human life: diets, work, villages and trade. Dairying favored adults who digest milk sugar. Knowledge of breeding and care is passed on as practice and as tradition.

entries.excludes: Domestication goes beyond selective breeding, because the relationship runs both ways. Early stages were often unplanned. Taming one animal changes its behavior within one lifetime and is not inherited. Claims about self-domestication of humans or other species are contested and left out.

entries.label: Innovation
entries.general: A new variant appears in a system that did not hold it before. It may arise by chance, by copying error, by recombining old parts or by deliberate effort. Whether it spreads is a separate question.

facets.biology: A new heritable variant arises as a change in DNA (mutation) or as a new combination of existing DNA (recombination). Mutations arise without regard to whether they would help.
facets.cognition: An individual finds a new solution to a problem, usually by trial and error and sometimes by apparent insight. Animals do this in many species, for example when they exploit a new food source. It can aim at a goal.
facets.culture: A new practice, word, belief or artifact enters a community's repertoire, by invention or by recombining old ideas. Many innovations are small changes to existing ones.
facets.technology: A new device, method or material is invented, often by combining existing parts or principles in a new way. Deliberate search and testing guide many inventions.
facets.AI and computation: Mutation randomly changes a candidate and crossover swaps parts between two candidates, producing new candidates. Some methods reward novelty itself, instead of the score or alongside it.

entries.excludes: Biological mutation ignores need, while human invention is often aimed at a goal. Chance may play a part in both. A new variant changes a population only after it is copied. Innovation does not imply improvement. Most mutations change nothing or do harm, and many inventions fail.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 9-10 Biologie topics on Mutation and Rekombination, topics on inventions in Technik and Geschichte, and any topic on how solutions are generated.

entries.label: Development
entries.general: Change in one individual over its own lifetime, in which later states build on earlier ones. It comes from growth and from interaction with the setting, and it often follows a typical sequence.

facets.biology: An organism grows from egg or seed to adult through cell division, specialization of cells and interaction with its surroundings. Genes and conditions together shape the outcome, and some traits respond to conditions during growth.
facets.cognition: A child's thinking, language and social understanding change with age and experience, often in a typical order. Maturation, social interaction and cultural learning all contribute.
facets.education: The progressive growth of a learner's knowledge, skills or competencies over time, often supported by instruction that is gradually withdrawn (scaffolding).
facets.AI and computation: Analogy only. Developmental robotics trains a robot in stages modelled on child development. The robot does not grow or mature, and its designers choose the stages.

entries.excludes: Development is not a kind of evolution. A growing organism does not evolve, and a population does not grow up. The link is causal: development turns inherited information into a body and responds to conditions, which shapes the variants selection sees. Software development is another sense.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 1-2 Sachunterricht (Entwicklungsstadien von Blütenpflanzen, Keimung und Wachstum), grade 8 Biologie (vorgeburtliche Entwicklung, Individualentwicklung), and learner growth in any subject.

entries.label: Agency
entries.general: The capacity of an entity to sense its setting and respond flexibly in pursuit of its own aims, so that its actions change what happens next. Intention is one form of this capacity, found in some domains.

facets.biology: Organisms act to keep themselves going: they seek food, choose habitats and change their surroundings. On the organismal-agency view, this needs no intention, planning or awareness. It alters the pressures later generations face (niche construction).
facets.culture: People act for reasons, plan and weigh options, but within limits set by resources, rules and other people's actions. Groups and organisations act through their members' decisions. Their choices can reproduce or change those limits over time.
facets.cognition: A person acts intentionally: forms intentions, plans ahead, regulates their own action and reflects on whether the plan works (Bandura's four core properties). This form of agency needs a represented goal.
facets.education: A learner sets goals, chooses strategies, monitors progress and takes responsibility for learning. Teachers support agency by giving meaningful choices and gradually reducing guidance.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: a software or robot agent senses its setting and selects actions to reach goals set by its designer. It holds no reasons of its own, and others can change its goals.

entries.excludes: Intention and reasons belong to the human and cognition senses and are absent in bacteria and plants. Software has designer-set goals. A species, evolution or a gene is not an agent. Organism agency does not make variants arise to meet a need. Agency comes in degrees.

entries.label: Transmission
entries.general: The process by which information, traits or practices move from one holder (organism, person, group or system) to another, so that the receiver ends up with something similar to what the sender had.

facets.biology: Genes pass from parents to offspring through eggs, sperm or cell division. Some microbes also pass genes sideways to unrelated cells. Parents can also pass on a made environment such as a nest or burrow.
facets.culture: Practices pass between people by social learning: from parents, from peers and from older non-relatives. Imitation, teaching and language carry them. Learners often rebuild what they learn, so practices can change in passing.
facets.technology: Designs pass by copying drawings, code or products, by training apprentices and by taking a device apart to see how it works. A copied file can be exact. A copied skill usually is not.
facets.AI and computation: Data and trained models are copied exactly between machines. A smaller model can also be trained to imitate a larger one (distillation), which passes on behavior without copying its inner parts.
facets.education: A teacher explains, demonstrates and sets tasks, and the learner rebuilds the knowledge. What arrives is the learner's own version, so understanding can differ from what was taught.

entries.excludes: Fidelity differs. DNA copying and file copying are nearly exact. Human learning often rebuilds what it receives. Biological transmission runs mainly from parent to offspring. Culture and technology also allow transmission between peers and from many sources. A learner brings prior ideas, so understanding can differ from what was taught.

entries.label: Adaptation
entries.general: A feature of a system that fits the demands of its setting, together with whatever process made it fit. The fit can be observed on its own. The process differs by domain: selection over generations, adjustment within a lifetime, or deliberate design.

facets.biology: A heritable trait that natural selection built for its function, such as camouflage. Angepasstheit (adaptedness) is the fit of structure to habitat seen today, whatever its origin. Adaptations are the fits that selection explains; other fits have other causes.
facets.culture: A practice or tool whose form suits local conditions. Researchers argue that this comes from keeping and copying variants that worked, as with ways of making toxic food crops safe to eat. Users often cannot say why it works.
facets.technology: A design whose features suit its use and operating conditions. It is reached by trying variants and copying those that perform, or by deliberate engineering. The measure of fit is the job the design must do.
facets.AI and computation: A candidate solution whose encoded features score well against a fixed objective, reached by rounds of variation, scoring and copying in an evolutionary algorithm. The designer picks the objective and so defines what counts as fit.
facets.cognition: A learner or animal revises behavior after experience so that it suits current conditions. The adjustment belongs to that individual and lasts at most one lifetime. Offspring do not inherit it.

entries.excludes: Fit today does not show that selection built it. A trait selected for another use, or a by-product, can also fit. Lifetime adjustment is not inherited. Individuals can adjust to need, but populations do not evolve traits because individuals need them. In design and computing a person sets the target.

entries.label: Fitness
entries.general: How well a variant does, compared with its alternatives, at being kept and passed on in a given setting. What is counted depends on the domain: offspring, adopters or a score.

facets.biology: Relative reproductive success: the average number of offspring that individuals of a type leave, compared with other types in the same setting. Strength or health matter only through their effect on offspring numbers.
facets.culture: How often a practice or belief is learned and kept by others, compared with rival variants. It depends on ease of learning, apparent usefulness and who holds it. A popular practice can harm those who adopt it.
facets.AI and computation: A number a program assigns to each candidate solution to show how well it meets the objective. The score decides which candidates are copied or varied next. The programmer usually defines it before the run starts.

entries.excludes: Biological fitness is estimated from offspring counts and depends on the environment. In computing a designer usually assigns it beforehand. Cultural success can follow learners' biases and can harm adopters. Fitness always compares a variant with rivals in a stated setting.

entries.label: Population
entries.general: A set of members counted together because they vary and affect one another's chances of being copied. Change over time is described as a shift in the mix of variants across the set. No single member needs to change for the set to change.

facets.biology: Interbreeding organisms of one species in a place and time. Members share a gene pool, so their alleles mix each generation. Evolution is a change in how common alleles or traits are in this group.
facets.culture: The people who can learn from one another, such as a village or an online community. Who copies whom sets the boundary, so one person belongs to several. Researchers count variants, such as first names or pottery styles.
facets.technology: All versions of a design in use or on record, such as the car models on the road or the pottery found at a site. Counts of each version show which designs spread or vanish.
facets.AI and computation: The pool of candidate solutions in an evolutionary algorithm. The programmer chooses its size, which usually stays fixed. Each round replaces the pool with a new one built from the better candidates.

entries.excludes: Interbreeding defines a biological population only. A cultural population is defined by who copies whom, and populations overlap. A program's population has a size set by the programmer. Population thinking treats differences among members as the data, so a population is never one typical member repeated.

entries.label: Drift
entries.general: Change in how common a variant is that comes from chance in which copies get passed on. It needs no advantage for the variant and is strongest in small populations. Drift can remove variants and can make rare variants common.

facets.biology: Allele frequencies shift from one generation to the next because the parents that happen to reproduce are a random sample. In small populations an allele can disappear or take over without any advantage.
facets.culture: When people copy at random from those around them, the popularity of baby names, pottery styles or other variants rises and falls by chance. Random-copying models fit several such records.
facets.technology: Which of several similar designs becomes common can depend on chance in early adoption. A random-copying model fits counts of technology patent applications, which suggests chance can decide this. Other processes could give the same counts.
facets.AI and computation: In a genetic algorithm with a small pool, features can spread or vanish by luck in which candidates get picked to reproduce, even when scores are equal. This can end the search early.

entries.excludes: A fit to a random-copying model does not prove random copying, because other processes can give the same counts. Many people copy with biases such as prestige, which acts like selection. Drift in computing comes from pool size. Drift acts on a set and never on one individual.

entries.label: Selection Pressure
entries.general: A factor that makes some variants more likely than others to be kept and passed on, and so sets the direction in which the mix of variants shifts. It acts on the mix across a population and gives individuals no push to change.

facets.biology: A feature of the surroundings or of other organisms that changes survival or reproduction of variants, such as predators, drought, disease, food supply or rivals for mates. Its strength shows in how much survival or reproduction differs among variants.
facets.culture: Conditions that make some practices easier to keep and pass on: climate and resources, laws and prices, and the learning biases of the people who copy, such as favoring prestigious models.
facets.AI and computation: In an evolutionary algorithm, selection pressure is how strongly the selection rule favors higher scorers, for example by letting only the best few of a random sample become parents. The programmer sets it, and high pressure reduces variety.

entries.excludes: In biology a pressure is a factor in the setting. In computing it is the strength of a rule a programmer chose, a different quantity. A pressure changes which variants are kept and makes no individual change or try to change. Cultural pressures include learners' own preferences.

entries.label: Extinction
entries.general: The end of a lineage: a kind of thing that was once passed on stops being passed on, so no later copies exist. Causes include loss of holders, failure to reproduce and an end to copying.

facets.biology: A species ends when its last member dies without leaving offspring. Common causes include habitat loss, climate change, hunting and disease.
facets.culture: A language goes extinct when its last speakers die or when the community stops passing it to children. Studies of thousands of languages test predictors such as road density and years of schooling.
facets.technology: A technique is lost when no one who can make it remains and no record survives. Tasmanian tool loss is debated: one model blames a small isolated population, and a later study doubts that population size explains such losses.

entries.excludes: A species cannot return, while languages and techniques can sometimes be revived from records and learners. Cultural loss does not need the holders to die, because they may adopt another language or tool. A fall in numbers is not yet extinction. Software and file-format obsolescence is left out.

entries.label: Descent
entries.general: Links between earlier and later versions through reproduction or copying, so that shared features can be traced to a shared origin. Where one line splits in two, descendants share an ancestor and differ by what changed afterwards. Relatedness can be drawn as a branching tree.

facets.biology: Organisms descend from parents. Two lineages that split from a common ancestor share inherited features, and the pattern of splits is drawn as a phylogenetic tree. Population splits can end in separate species.
facets.culture: Languages and hand-copied texts descend from earlier ones. Shared words or shared copying errors show which versions are related, and trees are rebuilt with methods borrowed from biology. Borrowing and mixing between lines also happens.
facets.technology: Designs descend from earlier designs, with features carried forward across versions. Family trees of artifacts can be drawn, but makers often combine features from different lines, which makes the pattern more like a network.

entries.excludes: Biological descent runs mostly from parent to offspring, so a tree fits well for most animals. Microbes, languages, texts and designs borrow across lines, so a tree fits only partly. Shared features can come from shared ancestry or from independent solutions. A tree has no ladder or main line.

entries.label: Differential Reproduction

facets.biology: Variants leave different numbers of offspring because of how they interact with their surroundings. Over generations this shifts which variants are common.
facets.culture: Variants are learned by different numbers of new holders, so some practices become common while others fade.
facets.AI and computation: Candidates are picked as parents at different rates according to their scores, so higher scorers leave more copies in the next round.

entries.excludes: The number of copies left is the criterion in biology and in algorithms that pick parents by score. In culture it is the number of new holders. Education and search methods without copies have no such count. Organisms do not try to leave offspring in order to evolve.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie 'Entstehung der Artenvielfalt' (Reproduktionserfolg, Fitness).
grounding: doi:10.1146/annurev.es.01.110170.000245 (Lewontin 1970, The units of selection; Crossref-checked)
ISBN 9780262631853 (Mitchell, An Introduction to Genetic Algorithms; Open Library-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Same idea as the biology sense of Selection: variants leave different numbers of offspring. The facets restate it as copies left, which also fits culture and computing.

entries.label: Sexual Selection

facets.biology: Variants differ in mating success because members of one sex compete for, or are chosen by, the other. Traits can spread by raising mating success even when they lower survival.

entries.excludes: Mate competition and mate choice are behaviors that shape selection, which links this to Agency. Neither needs planning for evolutionary ends. Only biology is drafted here. Other domains were not checked, so no facet is claimed for them.
entries.curriculumUse: Peacock plumage and similar cases used in evolution teaching; no Sachsen digest case found.
entries.reason: A case of selection where other members of the species do the choosing or competing. It fits Selection. Other domains have no documented process of this kind, so only biology gets a facet.

entries.label: Common Ancestor

facets.biology: The organism or population from which two or more later lineages split. Relatives share it, and branch points in the tree mark such ancestors.
facets.culture: An earlier language or text from which several later versions were copied or developed, such as a parent language. It is usually inferred from what the descendants share.

entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie Stammesgeschichte des Menschen (Hominidenstammbaum) and Zwischenformen.
grounding: doi:10.1038/29667 (Barbrook et al. 1998, The phylogeny of The Canterbury Tales; Crossref-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7602-1 (Biologie grade 10, Stammesgeschichte des Menschen; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: The branch point of Descent: the source of later versions. Handled as part of Descent, which also covers languages and texts.

entries.label: Phylogeny

facets.biology: The branching tree of relatedness among organisms, built from shared inherited features such as anatomy and DNA.
facets.culture: Language trees and text-family trees built from shared words or copying errors, using methods borrowed from biology.
facets.technology: Trees of artifact lineages built from shared design features. Borrowing across lines often makes the pattern more like a net than a tree.

entries.excludes: A tree shows relatedness. It does not rank branches, and it has no main line toward one group.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie Modell zum Hominidenstammbaum and Homologien.
grounding: Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7602-1 (Biologie grade 10, Stammesgeschichte des Menschen; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: The tree-drawing side of Descent. Language trees, manuscript trees and artifact trees use the same method, so one general concept carries all of them.

entries.label: Gene
entries.excludes: Whether a gene carries information in a strict sense is debated in the philosophy of biology. A cultural or computing counterpart of the gene as a discrete unit is contested and left out.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie Genetik (Speicherung, Weitergabe und Realisierung der Erbanlagen).
grounding: doi:10.1086/392768 (Maynard Smith 2000, The concept of information in biology; Crossref-checked)
entries.reason: The general idea a gene carries is stored information that is copied and read out. Information already names genetic encoding, so a biology facet there is enough. Gene itself stays a biology-only term.

entries.label: Allele

facets.biology: An allele is one alternative version of a gene. The mix of alleles in a population is its genetic variation, and a mutation creates a new allele.

entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie Genetik and the Mutation, Rekombination, Selektion factors in Entstehung der Artenvielfalt.
grounding: Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Alleles are one unit of biological variation. Variation already says differences among members, so a biology facet there covers alleles.

entries.label: Mutation

facets.biology: A heritable change in a DNA sequence, such as a swapped base, a deletion or a duplication. It creates a new genetic variant and arises without regard to whether it would help.
facets.AI and computation: A mutation operator randomly changes part of a candidate, standing in for DNA mutation. The programmer sets how often and how much.

entries.excludes: Mutation in biology ignores need. Human invention can aim at a goal, and the two should not be merged.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 9-10 Biologie Genetik and the Mutation, Rekombination, Selektion factors in Entstehung der Artenvielfalt.
grounding: ISBN 9780262631853 (Mitchell, An Introduction to Genetic Algorithms; Open Library-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Mutation is the biology case of generating a new variant, which Innovation names. The crosswalk already treated Innovation as broader.

entries.label: Heritable Variation

facets.biology: Differences among individuals in traits, some of which pass from parents to offspring through genes. Only the part that is passed on can build up over generations.
facets.culture: Differences in practices that others learn and so carry on. A habit that nobody copies is variation that ends with its holder.
facets.technology: Differences in design that are carried into later versions of a tool, machine or program.
facets.AI and computation: Differences stored in the encoded candidate, which the next round copies. Settings that are not copied do not count.

entries.excludes: Variation without heritability exists in every domain and cannot build up. Heritable variation in culture is made and changed on purpose as well as by error.
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie 'Entstehung der Artenvielfalt' and any topic that asks which differences get passed on.
grounding: doi:10.1146/annurev.es.01.110170.000245 (Lewontin 1970, The units of selection; Crossref-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Variation plus the condition that differences are passed on. That condition links Variation to Inheritance and is better stated inside Variation than as a second concept.

entries.label: Speciation
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 10 Biologie 'Veränderung der Arten und Artbildung' and the isolation case in Stammesgeschichte des Menschen stay in biology.
grounding: doi:10.1080/10635150701701083 (de Queiroz 2007, Species concepts and species delimitation; Crossref-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Defined by reproductive isolation between species, which has no counterpart in culture, technology or code. The branching idea is covered by Descent. Language splits lack an isolation test of this kind.

entries.label: Species
entries.curriculumUse: Grade 5 Biologie Artenkenntnis (Fische, Lurche, Kriechtiere, Vögel) and grade 10 Artbegriff stay in biology. Identification keys point to a separate classification idea.
grounding: doi:10.1080/10635150701701083 (de Queiroz 2007, Species concepts and species delimitation; Crossref-checked)
Sachsen Lehrplan topic lehrplan-522-1/lernbereich-7601-1 (Biologie grade 10, Entstehung der Artenvielfalt; read in the topic cache)
entries.reason: Species concepts conflict even within biology. Reproductive isolation has no counterpart in culture or code. Sachsen also uses Art for naming and identifying kinds, which is a classification task.

entries.label: Cooperation
entries.general: Parties act together so that each gains from the others' actions, and some mechanism keeps the arrangement going when a party could gain by holding back. The mechanism differs by domain.

facets.biology: Animals or other organisms help or work with partners, and selection has favoured the helping. It is kept going by shared interest in the result, relatedness, repeated dealings, or partner choice and sanctions. Examples: cooperative breeding, cleaner fish, pollination partnerships.
facets.culture: People coordinate on a task or shared resource. Trust, norms, incentives, reputation or institutions keep members contributing when free riding would pay. Examples: a village water scheme, a cooperative, an alliance between states, a school project team.
facets.AI and computation: Programs or robots pursue a joint result. A shared reward or a common protocol keeps each one contributing, and the designer sets it. Agents with separate rewards can face a free-rider temptation. Example: robot teams.

entries.excludes: Intention is needed in many human cases and absent in bees, cleaner fish and software. Hunting together is not always cooperation, because each animal may gain alone. Costly help to relatives counts only if gains to shared genes are included. Cooperation within a group can harm outsiders.
entries.curriculumUse: Lets one concept describe packs (Klasse 5), bee colonies (Klasse 6), pollination and cleaner partnerships (Klasse 9), cooperatives and Bismarck's alliances (Klasse 8), and team work in Informatik (Klassen 8, 10), each with its own sustaining mechanism.
grounding: DOI 10.1038/nature04755 (Bshary & Grutter 2006, cleaner fish, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1038/nature01931 (Kiers et al. 2003, host sanctions, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1046/j.1461-0248.2001.00218.x (Bronstein 2001, exploitation of mutualisms, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1086/284844 (Packer & Ruttan 1988, cooperative hunting, Crossref checked)
unverified: Leibo et al. 2017, Multi-agent reinforcement learning in sequential social dilemmas (AAMAS)
entries.reason: The general sentence names the benefit but drops what keeps cooperation going when holding back would pay, which Social-Core keeps. Adding it and three domain meanings also covers the animal and symbiosis cases.

entries.label: Conflict
entries.general: Two or more parties whose pursuits cannot all succeed at once, because they draw on the same limited resource or have incompatible aims. Parties can be organisms, species, people, groups or programs.

facets.biology: Competition and fighting. Individuals or species use the same limited food, space or mates, so one party's gain is another's loss. It can be indirect, with no contact, or direct, as in threat display, fights and territory defence.
facets.culture: People or groups hold opposed interests, values or goals and act on them, from arguments and strikes to war. They can negotiate, appeal to rules or use force. Conflict can end in settlement, domination or a standoff.
facets.AI and computation: Programs with opposed objectives, such as two game-playing agents where one's win is the other's loss. The designer builds the opposition into the objectives. The programs have no interests of their own.

entries.excludes: Competition between organisms needs no intention and can involve no contact. Predation and parasitism are one-sided and differ from competition. Persecution and bullying are one-sided harm, and calling them a clash of interests hides who acted. Software 'conflict' is a clash of operations.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes ecological Konkurrenz (Klasse 9), territory and aggression in mammals (Klasse 5), and war and resistance topics (Klassen 8 to 10). The excludes line guards the persecution and bullying cases (Ethik Klasse 6) against a two-sided reading.
grounding: ConceptBase NGSS competencies OE-COMPETENCY-000110 (MS-LS2-1) and OE-COMPETENCY-000148 (HS-LS4-2, competition for limited resources)
ConceptBase OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000016 (Social Dilemma: distinguishes aligned, mixed and fully opposed interests)
unverified: the computing facet rests on standard AI textbook material on zero-sum game search and on resource contention; no citation checked
entries.reason: The Interdisciplinary sentence can already hold ecological competition, but Social-Core's wording cannot. Naming competition on purpose, and separating it from predation and one-sided harm, settles the Konkurrenz case.

entries.label: Culture
entries.general: Behaviours, knowledge, beliefs and artifacts that group members acquire from one another by social learning (watching, listening to or copying others), that are typical of the group, and that persist as individual members come and go.

facets.biology: Group-typical behaviour that animals learn from others and pass on: chimpanzee tool use, regional bird dialects, humpback whale song. Documented in primates, birds, whales and fish. Cumulative build-up over generations is rare or debated.
facets.culture: Human culture adds language, symbols, shared norms and deliberate teaching. Knowledge, beliefs, practices and artifacts build up over generations, so a group holds more than any one member could invent alone (cumulative culture).
facets.AI and computation: Proposed extension. Systems trained on human cultural products carry patterns forward, and their outputs shape what people see and make next, which later systems learn from. Researchers call this machine culture. Whether machines learn socially is debated.

entries.excludes: Animal traditions lack, as far as is known, symbols, enforced norms and steady cumulative gain. Cultural differences between peoples are learned and show nothing about genetic differences, although culture and genes can affect each other (dairy farming and milk digestion). A culture has no fixed trait list.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes kulturelle Leistungen (China, Klasse 8) and citizenship education across eras (Klasse 6). Also gives a bounded way to place animal traditions as a contrast case to human culture.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000019 (Cumulative Culture) and OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000005 (Machine Culture)
DOI 10.1038/21415 (Whiten, Goodall, McGrew et al. 1999, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1073/pnas.1203179109 (Riedl et al. 2012, no third-party punishment in chimpanzees, Crossref checked)
entries.reason: Compared with Social-Core, the Interdisciplinary sentence drops no condition. It is wide enough to admit animal traditions and machine culture, so facets say where each fits and where it does not.

entries.label: Culture and Social Structure
entries.curriculumUse: Groups the social concepts. Animal groups are reached through Group, Role, Power, Cooperation and Conflict, and human rule systems through Norms and Institutions.
grounding: Organizing concept text read in the OpenLPM Interdisciplinary vocabulary on 2026-10-25
entries.reason: Organizing heading; the domain meanings sit on its child concepts. Its sentence names norms and institutions, which are mainly human, so read it as the human layer. List Group, Role and Power under it.

entries.label: Institutions
entries.general: Stable rules, written or unwritten, that a group recognises, together with the arrangements that apply them. They shape what members may, must or must not do and outlast any one member. This is mainly a human case.

facets.culture: Laws, constitutions, courts, schools, markets and customs. Formal institutions are written down and applied by officials. Informal ones are customs and conventions upheld by approval and disapproval (see Norms). People make, follow and change them.

entries.excludes: Law is a formal institution. Norms and conventions are the informal kind. Animal rank orders and policing belong under Group, Power and Cooperation, because no rule that members recognise is known. Software rules (protocols, permissions) cannot be broken, while laws and customs can, and people enforce them afterwards.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes law and constitutions (Klassen 8 to 10), traffic rules (Klassen 1 to 2), market forms (Klasse 8), class rules (Klasse 5) and public facilities. Protocols and access rules in Informatik can be compared as built-in rules.
grounding: DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511808678 (North 1990, formal and informal rules, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1038/nature04326 (Flack et al. 2006, policing in primates, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1038/342796a0 (Ratnieks & Visscher 1989, worker policing, Crossref checked)
unverified: Lessig 1999, Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace (software as a regulator)
entries.reason: The tagger could not tell whether formal law counts. Settled here: law is a formal institution and informal rules are Norms. The concept is mainly human, with a built-in-rules reading in computing.

entries.label: Norms
entries.general: A shared expectation within a group about how members should behave, upheld by the group's own approval, disapproval or exclusion. No formal authority is needed. This is mainly a human case.

facets.culture: Customs, manners, netiquette and religious duties, as held and upheld by a community. Members praise those who follow a norm and criticise or shun those who do not. Whether a norm is justified is an ethical question.
facets.cognition: In a person's mind, a rule of conduct taken on as one's own. The person expects to feel guilt or shame for breaking it and may follow it with nobody watching. One account of why people follow norms unwatched.

entries.excludes: Animal conformity is copying the majority, and no animal is known to expect that others ought to follow. Written law (Rechtsnorm) is an institution. A report of what a group expects differs from a claim that something ought to be done. Averages, Normwerte, DIN-Normen and the Reaktionsnorm are other senses.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes Netiquette and Umgangsformen, class and community rules, group pressure, and ethical demands of religions (Klassen 5 to 9). Separates these from descriptive versus normative statements in Biologie (Klassen 7 to 10).
grounding: ConceptBase AI4K12 OE-COMPETENCY-000528 (AI systems and the norms of the groups they serve)
DOI 10.1006/jtbi.2003.3104 (Gintis 2003, internalisation of norms, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1017/S0140525X14001356 (Norenzayan et al. 2016, religion and prosociality, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1038/nature04047 (Whiten et al. 2005, conformity in chimpanzees, Crossref checked)
entries.reason: Formal law goes to Institutions and Norms keep the informal part. Religious duties count when a community upholds them. Descriptive-versus-normative statements and statistical norms in Biologie are excluded on purpose.

entries.label: Collective Intelligence
entries.general: A group's combined output solves a problem or estimates a quantity better than a typical member could alone. How members' contributions are combined decides whether the group does better, and some ways of combining make it worse.

facets.biology: Animal groups reach good decisions or solutions through simple local interactions with no leader. Honeybee scouts compare nest sites and reach a quorum (enough scouts agree), and ant trails converge on short routes through pheromone reinforcement.
facets.culture: People pool estimates, skills or knowledge: averaging many guesses, team problem solving, science built on many researchers. Larger, well-connected populations may invent more (the collective brain; debated). Independent estimates help, while copying each other can spoil the result.
facets.AI and computation: Methods that combine many simple units: voting ensembles of models, ant-colony and swarm search. The designer writes the combining rule. Units need no understanding of the whole problem.

entries.excludes: Groups are not automatically smarter: copying, shared bias and a loud leader can make a crowd worse than its members (information cascades). Bees and ants have no leader and no plan, while human groups can plan and talk.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes colony-level problem solving and Arbeitsteilung in bees (Klasse 6), peer-to-peer and collaboration services in networks (Klassen 8 and 9), and team projects in Informatik (Klasse 10).
grounding: DOI 10.1126/science.1210361 (Seeley et al. 2012, honeybee swarms, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1073/pnas.0403723101 (Hong & Page 2004, Crossref checked; its result is debated)
unverified: Dorigo & Stützle 2004, Ant Colony Optimization (MIT Press)
entries.reason: The general sentence promises more than groups deliver: it omits that the combining rule decides the outcome and that crowds can fail. Adds biology, culture and computing meanings with the failure case in excludes.

entries.label: Communication
entries.general: A sender produces a signal, a receiver responds to it, and a code shared by both sides links the signal to the response. Whether anything is understood differs by domain.

facets.biology: A signal shaped by selection to change a receiver's behaviour, and a response shaped to read it: bird song, alarm calls, the honeybee dance. A cue carries information without being sent. No meaning is needed.
facets.culture: People exchange meaning through language, writing, images and gestures. Speakers intend to be understood, read each other's intentions and share conventions that can be learned and changed. Messages can mislead, and interpretation depends on context.
facets.technology: Devices exchange encoded messages over a channel under an agreed protocol, as in networks and telephony. The protocol fixes the format and the steps. A message can be delivered correctly with nobody understanding it, and noise can corrupt it.

entries.excludes: Meaning and intention are present in human language and may be absent in animal signals and machine messages. A cue is information that nobody sent. Delivering a message correctly differs from being understood. Signals are not always honest in any domain.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes bird song and the Sender-Empfänger-Modell (Klasse 5), bee communication (Klasse 6), media and propaganda, and network protocols and communication services (Informatik Klassen 8 and 9).
grounding: DOI 10.1111/j.1420-9101.2007.01497.x (Scott-Phillips 2008, Defining biological communication, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1017/S0140525X05000129 (Tomasello et al. 2005, shared intentions, Crossref checked)
unverified: Maynard Smith & Harper 2003, Animal Signals (Oxford University Press)
entries.reason: The sentence says 'between agents' and drops the human holder and the meaning that Social-Core keeps. A sender-signal-receiver-code structure covers animal and machine cases, and facets say where meaning is required.

entries.label: Group
entries.general: A set of individuals who interact with one another more than with outsiders, or who are treated as belonging together, so that membership affects who helps, shares with, competes with or excludes whom.

facets.biology: Animals that stay together and interact repeatedly (sozialer Verband): packs, troops, insect colonies. Members may know one another as individuals, and insects use colony smell. Group life brings gains such as defence and costs such as competition.
facets.culture: People who see themselves, or are seen by others, as one body with shared interests or identity: families, school classes, parties, nations. Members need not meet. Membership can be chosen, inherited, or assigned by outsiders, sometimes against a person's will.

entries.excludes: Animal groups can carry markers such as colony smell. Belonging needs no shared identity. A bee colony has no ruler: the queen lays eggs and does not command. In animals, a population or a chance crowd is a group only if members interact. Human groups can rest on identity alone.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes the bee colony as sozialer Verband (Klasse 6), packs and herds (Klasse 5), and parties, interest groups and nationalist movements (Klassen 8 and 9) with one concept and stated differences.
grounding: DOI 10.1146/annurev.es.05.110174.001545 (Alexander 1974, evolution of social behaviour, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1002/ejsp.2420010202 (Tajfel et al. 1971, social categorization, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1126/science.1210361 (Seeley et al. 2012, colony decisions without a ruler, Crossref checked)
entries.reason: Social-Core has Group and the Interdisciplinary space has none. Animal social groups (sozialer Verband) are well documented, so the concept travels to biology. Computing offers only clusters and sets, so no facet is given there.

entries.label: Role
entries.general: A recurring position in a group's division of labour, with typical behaviour attached. Who fills it, and whether they can change position, differs by domain.

facets.biology: Social insect castes and age-linked tasks, and helpers in cooperative breeders. In honeybees, workers shift from nursing to foraging as they age. Roles arise from development or age, and a caste can be fixed for life.
facets.culture: A position such as teacher, parent, judge or citizen. Other people expect certain behaviour from whoever holds it, and sanction departures. People are assigned, choose, train for or inherit roles, and can hold several at once.
facets.AI and computation: Named positions in a system: client and server in a network, administrator and user in an access scheme. The role fixes what its holder may do, and any machine or account can hold it.

entries.excludes: Insect individuals do not accept or refuse a role. Human roles carry expectations and sanctions and can be negotiated. 'Caste' also names a hereditary human social class, a different thing. Software roles carry no expectations or feelings.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes Arbeitsteilung in bees (Klasse 6), roles in groups and society (Ethik and Gemeinschaftskunde), and client-server versus peer-to-peer roles in Informatik (Klasse 9).
grounding: DOI 10.1146/annurev.en.37.010192.003225 (Robinson 1992, division of labour in insects, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1109/2.485845 (Sandhu et al. 1996, role-based access control, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1023/A:1010071910869 (Wooldridge, Jennings & Kinny 2000, roles for software agents, Crossref checked)
entries.reason: Division of labour gives Role a documented non-human reading (insect castes, helpers) and a designed one in computing. Expectations and sanctions stay human, and the excludes line says so.

entries.label: Incentive
entries.general: A benefit or cost attached to an option that changes how often the option is chosen. How the effect arises differs by domain: through expectation and judgement, through learning, or through an update rule.

facets.culture: Prices, wages, grades, fines, praise and taxes. People weigh expected gains and costs, along with fairness, reputation and values. Material incentives can backfire: a fine for lateness can make lateness more common if it turns a duty into a price.
facets.biology: Animals shift their choices toward options with higher payoffs: foraging animals leave a patch when the gain rate falls, and rewarded actions are repeated (reinforcement). Evolution shapes which payoffs matter. The animal needs no idea of why.
facets.AI and computation: A reward signal returned after an action. A learning program changes its behaviour to collect more reward. People set the reward, so a badly chosen reward is followed faithfully, including in unintended ways.

entries.excludes: People can offer and understand an incentive. Animals and learning programs respond to payoffs without understanding them. Payoffs in evolution change which strategies persist across generations, which is selection. They do not change one individual's choice. Money is one kind of incentive. Approval and fairness also move people.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes market coordination through prices, supply and demand (Gemeinschaftskunde Klassen 8 and 10), reward-based learning in AI units, and foraging choices in animal behaviour.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000023 (Homo Economicus: material incentives can backfire)
ConceptBase AI4K12 OE-COMPETENCY-000399 (reinforcement learning) and OE-COMPETENCY-000341 (maximizing reward)
DOI 10.1086/468061 (Gneezy & Rustichini 2000, A fine is a price, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1016/0040-5809(76)90040-X (Charnov 1976, marginal value theorem, Crossref checked)
unverified: Amodei et al. 2016, Concrete problems in AI safety (reward misspecification)
entries.reason: Social-Core's Incentive has no match, and the education sense of Selection says nothing about what makes an option attractive. Payoff-driven choice is documented in animals and in learning software, so the concept travels with care.

entries.label: Power
entries.general: The ability of one party to affect another party's options or outcomes, for example by controlling something the other needs, by force, or by shaping what the other believes. The ability belongs to the relationship between the parties.

facets.biology: Dominance: in a pair, one animal reliably gets first access to food, mates or space, because of past contest wins, size, age or inherited rank, and a threat now suffices. Ranks form an order in the group (Rangordnung).
facets.culture: People hold power through force, control of money or resources, authority accepted as rightful, or influence over what others know and believe. Rulers, employers, owners, media and states all have it. Power can be limited by law, institutions and resistance.

entries.excludes: Legitimacy, authority and law belong to human cases. Animal dominance does not rest on any rule that members accept. In wild wolf packs the 'alpha' pair are the parents, so rank follows family position. Animal rank orders give no reason for human hierarchies. Shaping beliefs is mainly a human case.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes Rangordnung in mammals (Klasse 5), media manipulation (Ethik Klasse 7), colonial influence on borders and oil as an economic and political factor (Geographie Klasse 7), with the animal reading's limits stated.
grounding: DOI 10.1002/bs.3830020303 (Dahl 1957, The concept of power, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1163/156853993X00290 (Drews 1993, dominance in animal behaviour, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1139/z99-099 (Mech 1999, alpha status in wolf packs, Crossref checked)
ConceptBase OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000022 (Egalitarianism: leveling mechanisms against dominance)
entries.reason: Power has a thin but documented animal reading in dominance and rank order, which Klasse 5 teaches. Authority, legitimacy and control of beliefs stay human, so the general sentence is relational and excludes names what does not transfer.

entries.label: Diffusion
entries.general: Something spreads through a population because holders pass it to others they are in contact with. The pattern of spread depends on who is in contact with whom and on what makes a contact pass it on.

facets.biology: A pathogen passing between hosts, or a learned behaviour spreading along an animal group's social ties, such as a new foraging trick in wild birds or lobtail feeding in humpback whales. Infection needs no choice by the host.
facets.culture: An idea, practice or technology spreads as people see it, hear of it and adopt it. Adoption often follows an S-shaped curve, with early adopters first. People adopt for many reasons: benefit, prestige, pressure or chance.
facets.AI and computation: A file, message or program copy spreads over a network, or a node adopts a state when enough neighbours have. Simple rules on a contact network can reproduce epidemics and viral posts. A designer writes the passing-on rule.

entries.excludes: Wide spread does not show that the thing is better or fitter. Spread can follow popularity, prestige or chance. One hand-over is Transmission, and Diffusion is the pattern across a population. Selection needs a reason some variants spread more, such as fit to the setting. Diffusion needs only contact.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes the spread of industrialisation from England (Geschichte Klasse 8), of customs between communities, of infections between hosts, and of data across networks in Informatik.

entries.curriculumUse: Topics such as the shift from agrarian to service society (Geographie Klasse 10) and industrialisation (Geschichte Klasse 8) stay describable through Culture, Institutions, Technology and Evolutionary Process. The gap is a recorded difference between the spaces.
