entries.label: Knowledge
entries.general: Information that a holder has kept, has grounds to rely on and can use to act or to answer questions. The holders are people and groups. The kind of grounds differs by domain.

facets.cognition: What a person has learned and keeps, including facts, concepts and know-how. It guides action and reasoning. People can often give reasons, and know-how is backed by a track record even when they cannot.
facets.culture: Understanding a group holds and justifies together through shared records, expertise and checks such as evidence, peer review and source criticism. No member holds all of it. It outlasts its members when written down or taught.
facets.education: The facts, concepts and procedures a curriculum selects for learners, which teaching tries to turn into understanding the learner can use. Knowing facts differs from applying them, so curricula also name skills and competences.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: a knowledge base stores statements that a program searches to answer questions. People wrote or checked them and quality varies. The program has no grounds of its own. Whether a trained model's patterns count is debated.

entries.excludes: Information in genes, a library or a model's weights is knowledge only when a holder can use it and has grounds to rely on it. Genes and immune memory were shaped by selection, and no holder checked them. A group can share a mistake, so agreement alone is not enough.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes knowledge in history source work (limits of interpreting sources), curriculum goals about what students should know, and school topics on memory. Gives knowledge-base topics in informatics a flagged technical reading.
grounding: ConceptBase AI4K12 OE-COMPETENCY-000263 (what an agent must know)
DOI 10.1145/3447772 (Hogan et al. 2021, Knowledge Graphs, Crossref checked)
DOI 10.1093/analys/23.6.121 (Gettier 1963, Crossref verified; background on justification)
entries.reason: Adds domain meanings. The current wording lets any system hold knowledge, which invites machine attribution. Holders are narrowed to people and groups, and the machine reading becomes a flagged technical facet.

entries.label: Collective Action

facets.culture: Many people must contribute to a shared good, such as a clean river, and each can gain by letting others pay. Commons, taxes and public goods raise this problem. Rules, monitoring, sanctions and trust are the usual answers.
facets.biology: Individuals produce something that benefits all nearby members, and non-producers gain without paying. Pathogenic bacteria release iron-scavenging molecules, and cheaters that do not make them can spread unless relatedness or other checks limit them.

entries.excludes: Collective action names a problem and cooperation is one way it ends. When interests align there is no dilemma. Free riding needs no intention in bacteria.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes shared-resource problems such as commons and public goods in Gemeinschaftskunde and Ethik, and partnerships such as cleaner fish where cheating is possible, with one problem statement across domains.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000016 (Social Dilemma) and OE-SANDBOX-CONCEPT-000017 (Tragedy of the Commons)
LiteratureBase OE-LITERATURE-koomen-herrmann-2018 and OE-LITERATURE-leighton-2014 (teaching the commons)
entries.reason: Collective Action names the free-rider problem that Cooperation's sustaining mechanisms answer. ConceptBase holds a general Social Dilemma sense, so it fits as domain meanings of Cooperation. Merge with Cooperation's own facets.

entries.label: Information
entries.general: A pattern that varies in step with something else. A receiver that can use that link becomes less uncertain about the other thing, or can act on it. Receivers include cells, animals, people and machines.

facets.biology: Pattern: a gene's base sequence, a hormone level or an animal signal. Receiver: the cell's machinery, an organ or another animal. Accounts differ on whether genes carry meaning or only cause effects. School biology rarely measures it in bits.
facets.cognition: Pattern: sensory input or a stored trace. Receiver: a nervous system whose later expectations and actions change. Memory is partly rebuilt at each recall, so a stored trace is not a copy of the input.
facets.culture: Pattern: words, pictures, records or media. Receiver: a person who reads them with shared codes. Meaning and truth matter here, so a message can mislead and its source needs checking.
facets.AI and computation: Pattern: a message chosen from a known set of possible messages. Receiver: a decoder built around the odds of each message. The less likely the message, the more bits it carries. Meaning plays no part.

entries.excludes: Bits measure information only where the possible messages and their odds are known. Meaning and truth play no part in the bit count, yet both matter in human communication. Animal tracks and tree rings carry information although nobody meant to send it. Uncertainty here counts possibilities for any receiver.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes the Sachsen biology organizing field 'Information' (senses, hormones, genes, brain memory), informatics 'Informationen und Daten' with bits and units, and the source-checking topics in media, history and geography.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000108 (NGSS MS-LS1-8, sensory receptors and memory)
entries.reason: Adds facets and repairs the general sentence. Source, pattern and receiver travel across domains. Bits, meaning, truth and a sender do not. Meaning enters only with human communication.

entries.label: Representation
entries.general: Something that stands in for something else, so that people can think about, talk about or act on the second thing through the first, and programs can process it. What makes it a stand-in differs by domain: shared structure, agreed conventions or learning history.

facets.cognition: Mental structures such as images, concepts and schemas that stand for things and let a person reason about them when they are absent. They are largely built from experience and can be partial or wrong.
facets.culture: Shared sign systems such as words, writing, numerals, maps and diagrams. A community agrees what the signs stand for, and the choice of system changes what is easy to say, calculate or notice.
facets.education: Maps, diagrams, tables and models used to teach. Learners must learn the conventions and see that a map is a simplified stand-in for a place. Reading and making representations is taught as a skill.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: tables, code, vectors and recorded values (data) that a program stores and processes as standing for something. Data become information only for a receiver who can read them. People supply the meaning.

entries.excludes: A shared or computed stand-in works only for a user who treats it as one, so the same marks can stand for different things. Brains use mental representations without anyone treating them as stand-ins. A map is not the territory; a stored vector means nothing to the program alone.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes map work in geography and Sachunterricht (the map as a generalized picture), number systems, markup languages and binary coding in informatics, and mental images or concepts in cognition topics.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000283 (AI4K12: the map is not the territory)
DOI 10.1007/s10539-006-9046-6 (Shea 2007, Crossref verified; representation in inheritance systems, background only)
entries.reason: Adds domain meanings and a general sentence that names the user and conventions, which the current text leaves out. Names who supplies the meaning in each domain.

entries.label: Data

facets.AI and computation: Data: recorded values such as numbers, text or pixels, stored so a program can process them. They stand for measurements or events and become information only for a receiver who can read them.

entries.curriculumUse: Covers data protection, databases, binary data and data analysis in informatics, and measurement tables in science topics. Every digest case fits the narrow sense, so no separate Interdisciplinary entry is needed.
entries.reason: Data is a recorded kind of representation. Every Sachsen case tagged for it fits the narrow sense, so a separate general entry adds a word and no new structure.

entries.label: Learning
entries.general: A lasting change in how an individual or system acts or responds, brought about by experience. Experience may be direct, observed in others or arranged by a teacher or designer.

facets.cognition: A person changes what they know, expect or can do because of experience. The change is stored in the nervous system, lasts, and shapes later action. It can be accurate or wrong, and it includes learning from other people.
facets.biology: Many animals change behavior through experience: habituation, association, trial and error and copying others. The change happens within one lifetime and, in nervous systems, rests on altered connections between nerve cells. Change across generations by selection is a separate process.
facets.culture: Newcomers take on a group's norms, roles and knowledge by taking part in its activities and being instructed. The change is described as growing participation. What changes is a person's skill and place in the group.
facets.education: A learner meets planned experiences, and the change is judged against stated goals. Prior ideas shape what is learned. The result can be new knowledge, a skill or a revised belief, and it can fade without practice.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: a procedure adjusts a model's numbers from example data or trial outcomes so that a designer-chosen score improves. Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement methods differ in their feedback. No understanding is implied.

entries.excludes: In machine learning what changes is a set of numbers, and no understanding is implied. Many trained models stay fixed until retrained. Evolution changes populations over generations, while learning changes one individual; some theories link the two as selection. Fatigue or injury can change behavior without learning.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes learning in Sachunterricht (learning from mistakes, learning together), human and animal learned behavior in biology, and machine learning in informatics grade 9 under a flagged technical reading.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000358 (AI4K12 3-5: people and computers both learn from patterns, people are flexible)
ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000360 (AI4K12 6-8: human learning versus machine learning)
ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000394 (AI4K12 9-12: algorithms adjust internal representations)

TheoryBase OE-CROSSDOMAINCONSTRUCT-selection-as-hierarchical-bayesian-updating (theory bridge: the record treats learning and evolution as one kind of updating at different grains and does not claim they are identical)
entries.reason: Facets and excludes settle the shared word: in living things knowledge or skill changes, in machine learning a parameter set changes. Machine Learning folds in as a flagged technical facet.

entries.label: Machine Learning

facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: a procedure adjusts a model's numbers from example data or trial outcomes so that a score chosen by designers improves. Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement methods differ in the feedback they use. No understanding is implied.

entries.curriculumUse: Covers the informatics grade 9 topic on artificial intelligence (supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, data basis, model) and the grade 10 AI web application project. Both fit the narrow sense.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000362 (AI4K12 9-12: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning)
ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000394 (AI4K12 9-12: algorithms adjust internal representations)
entries.reason: Machine Learning shares the word with Learning and differs in what changes. It fits better as one flagged technical facet of Learning than as a second general concept.

entries.label: Teaching
entries.general: Behavior by one individual or system that responds to another's learning needs and helps that other acquire a skill or piece of knowledge sooner or more reliably than it would alone.

facets.biology: Meerkat adults give pups prey in forms matched to the pups' age, which improves the pups' skill. Researchers test the behavior pattern and its cost to the adult. They do not need to know whether the adult intends to teach.
facets.cognition: On one account, adults signal that a demonstration is meant to teach, using eye contact and infant-directed speech. Infants are tuned to these signals and then treat what is shown as general knowledge.
facets.education: A teacher plans tasks, explains, checks understanding and adjusts to the class. Intention and a stated learning goal are present. Success is judged by what students can do later.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: tutoring software picks tasks, hints and feedback from a student's answers by rules or learned patterns. People designed it to fill a teaching role. The software has no intent that the student understand.

entries.excludes: Intention to teach is part of human teaching. Animal studies test only the behavior pattern and its cost to the teacher. Setting an example without regard to who is watching is modeling. Tutoring software has no intent. Learners can learn with no teacher present.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes teaching in school topics such as learning together in Sachunterricht, and lets the biology grade 10 topic on learned behavior separate teaching from learning alone.
entries.reason: Repairs the general sentence by removing 'intentional', which fails for animal teaching studies. Intention moves to the education facet and the excludes. Adds four domain meanings.

entries.label: Scaffolding
entries.curriculumUse: Stays available for school tasks with hints or worked examples that fade. No Sachsen digest case needs a wider reading.
grounding: DOI 10.1111/j.1469-7610.1976.tb00381.x (Wood, Bruner and Ross 1976, Crossref verified)
entries.reason: Scaffolding is defined by support that is matched to a learner and fades as skill grows, which is a teacher-learner practice. Cross-domain cases of matched support sit in the Teaching facets. The education meaning stays.

entries.label: Metacognition
entries.general: A thinker's monitoring and control of its own thinking: judging how well it knows or understands something, noticing when a strategy fails and switching to another.

facets.cognition: People judge how well they know something, how hard a task is and whether to keep going. These judgments guide study and problem solving. They can be miscalibrated, with too much or too little confidence. Young children show early forms.
facets.education: Learners plan, check and revise their own work. Teachers prompt this with questions such as 'How do I know I understand?' and model it aloud. It is often taught as a strategy meant to apply across subjects.
facets.biology: Comparative studies test whether monkeys, apes and a few other animals decline difficult trials, which may reflect tracking their own uncertainty. Simpler explanations, such as learned cues, are also proposed. Whether any awareness is involved is debated.

entries.excludes: Knowing facts about thinking differs from controlling thinking in the moment. Confidence is not accuracy. Declining a hard trial may reflect monitoring and may show no awareness. A machine's confidence score is a computed number and shows no awareness of its own thinking.
entries.curriculumUse: No digest case tags it. Typical use is school goals about reviewing one's own work and strategies, and the OpenEvo content anchor Our Mind.
grounding: DOI 10.1017/S0140525X03000086 (Smith, Shields and Washburn 2003, Crossref verified)
entries.reason: Adds cognition, education and a debated comparative-animal facet. No machine facet is offered, because a confidence score is an engineered number and the excludes says so.

entries.label: Theory of Mind
entries.general: Representing another agent's goals, beliefs or knowledge, and using that to interpret and predict what it will do. The represented states can differ from the facts and from one's own.

facets.cognition: Children come to predict actions from what another person believes, including false beliefs, at about four to five years in standard tasks. Earlier forms track goals and attention.
facets.biology: Studies ask whether apes and other animals anticipate actions from what another sees, wants or believes. Evidence is stronger for goals and perception than for false belief, and the question remains debated.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: agent-modeling programs estimate another agent's goals from its behavior to predict its next move. Language models are tested on false-belief stories. Passing such tests shows how their text output behaves and settles nothing about inner states.

entries.excludes: Mental-state attributions can be wrong, and the attributed state can differ from the facts. Predicting an agent's behavior does not show that the predictor feels, understands or wants anything. Passing or failing one test, in children, animals or language models, may not carry over to other tasks.
entries.curriculumUse: No digest case tags it. Typical use is child development, comparing animal and human social thinking, and perspective-taking topics such as understanding others in Ethik grade 6.
grounding: DOI 10.1111/1467-8624.00304 (Wellman, Cross and Watson 2001, Crossref verified)
DOI 10.1038/s41562-024-01882-z (Strachan et al. 2024, Crossref verified; tests of language models and humans on theory-of-mind tasks)
entries.reason: Adds a neutral general sentence that does not make human minds the default, plus cognition, animal and flagged machine readings. The machine facet is separated by wording and by the excludes.

entries.label: Intuitive Theories
entries.general: Informal, domain-specific explanations of how things work, such as folk physics, folk biology and folk psychology, formed before and outside instruction.

facets.cognition: Young children expect objects to fall, living things to grow from inside and people to act on wants. These expectations support explanation and prediction, and they change with age and evidence.
facets.education: Students arrive with ideas such as 'organisms change because they need to'. Instruction can build on them, revise them or compete with them, and they often resurface under time pressure even after the science is learned.
facets.culture: Communities share folk theories, for example about illness or inheritance, and pass them on through talk and practice. Content differs across cultures, while some early expectations recur widely.

entries.excludes: Intuitive theories are often useful and need not be wrong. Intuitive means formed without instruction and does not mean innate. They differ from formal models, which are stated openly and tested. Purpose-based explanations are common and do not show a learner is careless.
entries.curriculumUse: No digest case tags it. Typical use is teaching that starts from student preconceptions, such as purpose-based explanations of traits in evolution lessons.
entries.reason: Adds cognition, education and culture meanings and a shorter neutral general sentence. The excludes separates informal theories from formal models and from innate ideas.

entries.label: Analogical Reasoning
entries.general: Using a familiar case to understand a new one by matching the relations between their parts, then checking which matches hold and where the match breaks.

facets.cognition: A reasoner recalls a familiar case, maps its relational structure onto the new case and carries over inferences. Matching on shared relations gives better analogies than matching on appearance.
facets.education: Teachers and students build analogies and check where they fail, for example comparing breeders' choices with natural selection. Listing what maps and what breaks guards against false carry-over.
facets.culture: One proposal holds that analogies help complex ideas pass between people with less distortion, which supports cumulative cultural change. Scientists also move ideas between fields by analogy.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: programs such as the structure-mapping engine match relational descriptions of a known case and a new case and score the match. People write the descriptions. The program follows a stated procedure and claims no insight.

entries.excludes: Analogy needs matching relations, and surface resemblance alone does not count. Every analogy breaks somewhere. A mapping proposes a hypothesis and needs separate evidence. A program that scores a match is not reasoning as a person does. Cross-domain analogies, such as selection in biology and culture, need stated break points.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes analogy-based teaching, such as breeders' selection as a way into natural selection. No Sachsen digest case tags it directly.
grounding: DOI 10.1016/0004-3702(89)90077-5 (Falkenhainer, Forbus and Gentner 1989, Crossref verified)
DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2021.03.002 (Brand, Mesoudi and Smaldino 2021, Crossref verified)
entries.reason: Shortens the general sentence to the word limit and adds domain meanings. The excludes states the break-point rule that cross-domain analogies, including this space's own, need.

entries.label: Distributed Cognition
entries.general: Thinking or remembering carried out by a system of several people and tools, so that the whole system does the task and no single member holds all of it.

facets.cognition: In an airliner cockpit, the pilots, a speed card, the markers on the speed dial and their talk together set and remember the speeds needed for landing. Each holds a part. The unit of study is the whole cockpit system.
facets.technology: Notes, calculators, maps, search tools and AI assistants hold part of a person's task, and their design shapes how the person thinks. The tool stores and transforms information for a goal the person holds.
facets.culture: Teams, institutions and written records let a community remember and decide beyond any member's capacity, and they pass tasks on to newcomers.

entries.excludes: A tool in the system stores and transforms information but holds no goals of its own. A network of computers is a distributed system and counts here only when it serves a human thinking task. Groups can also think worse than their best member.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes personal memory aids in Sachunterricht grades 1 and 2, media and databases used as outside memory, and teamwork on shared tasks. No digest case tags it directly.
grounding: DOI 10.1145/353485.353487 (Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh 2000, Crossref verified)
entries.reason: Adds cognition, technology and culture meanings. The cognition facet stays separate from the Distributed System entry, so a computer network is not called cognition.

entries.label: Technology
entries.general: Tools, techniques and systems that individuals or groups make or adopt to extend what they can do. Designs can be passed on, improved and combined over time.

facets.technology: Engineers and makers design a tool or system to meet stated needs, build it, test it and revise it. Tests compare the result with the needs, and trade-offs are named.
facets.culture: Technologies are shared practices as well as objects: skills, materials and know-how pass on by teaching and imitation, and improvements accumulate across generations and shape how groups live and work.
facets.biology: Some animals make and use tools, such as New Caledonian crows shaping hooks from twigs. Designs differ between groups and may be learned from others. Whether improvements accumulate is debated.
facets.education: As a school subject, technology is designing, making and evaluating objects. It also covers digital tools for learning. Students judge a design by whether it meets its requirements.
facets.AI and computation: Technical reading: AI systems are tools that process data to give outputs for users who set the goals. The system has no purpose of its own.

entries.excludes: Technology has purposes set by makers and users. An artifact holds none of its own. Animal tool use may lack planning and accumulation. Technology is not always digital or new. A tool can extend one capacity and weaken another.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes Technik und Computer grades 5 and 6 (designing, making and evaluating objects, work plans), tool use in human origins (biology grade 10) and industrialisation (history grade 8).
entries.reason: The general sentence now allows animal tool traditions and does not require human makers. Adds technology, culture, biology, education and a flagged AI facet. Specification folds in here.

entries.label: Abstraction
entries.general: Leaving out detail so that what matters for some use stays in view. The leaving-out can be chosen, as in a map or a software layer, or happen without choice, as when a concept forms from many instances.

facets.cognition: Forming a concept or schema by dropping differences among instances, as 'bird' from many birds. The abstract relational structure of a case is what an analogy carries to another case.
facets.culture: Maps, diagrams and summaries leave out detail on purpose. Mapmakers generalize coastlines and roads so the picture serves one use, and a different use needs different detail.
facets.education: Students move from drawing a map of their school to asking what each kind of map keeps and leaves out, and later to describing a game board or a concept by its essential parts.
facets.AI and computation: Hiding how something works behind an interface, so that users and other parts need only know what it does. Layers each hide the one below, and the chosen level of detail is a design decision.

entries.excludes: What is left out suits one use and may matter for another. Everyday 'abstract' often means vague or hard to picture; abstraction here is exact about what it keeps. In concept formation it is often unconscious. In computing it is a deliberate design choice.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes the geography topic on the map as a generalized picture of reality (grade 5), simplified models in several subjects, and layers and interfaces in informatics. All four digest cases fit the narrow sense.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000284 (AI4K12 3-5: different maps capture different aspects)
ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000286 (AI4K12 6-8: a game board described in plain language)
entries.reason: Dropping detail for a purpose shows up in concept formation, mapmaking, school map work and software design, with different mechanisms. The Interdisciplinary space has no concept for it, though analogy depends on it.

entries.label: Algorithm
entries.general: A fixed series of steps that a person or machine can follow to get from a given start to a result.

facets.AI and computation: Finite, unambiguous steps a machine can execute with no judgment, turning input into output. A program is an algorithm written in a language the machine can run. Correctness and step counts can be checked.
facets.education: Step-by-step procedures taught in school, such as long division, a recipe or a key that asks one yes-or-no question per step to name a plant. Students test whether each step is clear enough that anyone could follow it without guessing.
facets.technology: A work plan or production sequence lists operations in order with tools and materials. Workers may need judgment at a step, so it meets the strict test only if every step is exact.

entries.excludes: A strict algorithm has finite, exact steps and needs no judgment, and many recipes and work plans fail that test. A natural process described as an algorithm has no author and no list of steps. A procedure that runs is not shown to be correct or fast.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes informatics grade 7 and 8 algorithm topics including transfer to everyday cases, dichotomous keys in biology grades 6 and 9, and the work plan in Technik und Computer grades 5 and 6.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000321 (AI4K12 3-5: an algorithm chooses the next move)
entries.reason: School topics apply the term to recipes, keys and work plans. A general 'fixed series of steps' reading lets students test which procedures meet the strict conditions. The biology facet is a modeling reading.

entries.label: Decomposition
entries.curriculumUse: The Sachsen case on splitting data into packets in networks stays at the Comp-Core level. Division of labour in insect colonies belongs with the cooperation concepts.
grounding: DOI 10.1145/1118178.1118215 (Wing 2006, Crossref verified; names decomposition among computational thinking moves)
entries.reason: Splitting a problem needs a solver who chooses the split, and that move is the same wherever it is used. Modularity in nature or machines is a property of systems and belongs with a systems concept.

entries.label: Feedback
entries.general: Information about a system's own output is returned to the system, so that its later behavior depends on its earlier results. The loop can damp a change or amplify it.

facets.biology: Body systems hold conditions near a range with loops: receptors detect a change, a control center compares it with a set range and organs respond, as insulin lowers blood sugar after a meal.
facets.technology: A controller compares a measured output with a target and adjusts the input, as a thermostat does. Designers choose the target, the sensor and the size of the correction.
facets.education: Information about a learner's work, goal and gap that the learner uses to improve the next attempt. A grade or comment becomes feedback only when the learner acts on it.
facets.AI and computation: Training loops compare a model's output with a target or reward and adjust its numbers. Deployed systems can also feed their outputs back into the data they later learn from, which can amplify errors.

entries.excludes: In everyday speech positive feedback means praise and negative feedback means criticism. In systems, negative feedback damps change and positive feedback amplifies it, whatever the tone. A comment the learner never uses is no loop. Late feedback can cause swings.
entries.curriculumUse: Describes the biological control loop for blood sugar (biology grade 8) and feedback to learners as used in lessons. The blood sugar case tags as narrower under Comp-Core.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000128 (NGSS HS-LS1-3: feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis)
ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000397 (AI4K12 3-5: a reinforcement signal lets a computer learn from experience)
DOI 10.1086/286788 (Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow 1943, Crossref verified)
entries.reason: A loop from output back to input is documented in body regulation, control engineering, teaching and training. The school sense of feedback as comment differs, so the excludes spells out the loop condition and the everyday tone words.

entries.label: Model
entries.general: A simplified stand-in for a system, built for a purpose, that people use to explain, predict or explore the system. It is judged by its fit to that purpose and can be revised.

facets.education: School models include scale models, diagrams, analogies, equations and simulations. Students use them to explain a phenomenon, learn that a model leaves features out, and test and improve it, for example by changing a simulation's settings.
facets.biology: Biologists use diagrams, equations and trees as models. A tree of human ancestors states which lineages share ancestors, and new fossils or DNA can revise it.
facets.culture: Geographers and economists use models such as the sector model of an economy or a model of a North American city region. They sort cases into types and state how parts relate. Places in the world differ from the model.
facets.cognition: On one account, a mental model is a person's internal, simplified stand-in used to reason about how something works. It can be incomplete or wrong, and it may run as a mental simulation.
facets.AI and computation: A formal description a computer can run: rules, equations or a fitted function whose numbers were set from data. Running it forward (a simulation) shows what follows; changing settings and rerunning shows what results depend on.

entries.excludes: A model is not the system, and one built for a purpose may fail for another. A role model is an example to copy, a different sense of the word. Scientific models face tests against evidence. Ethics lessons also call worldviews and accounts of conscience models, judged by other standards.
entries.curriculumUse: Covers the hominid family tree, sector and city-region models, conscience models, the input-process-output model and scale models. Worldview 'models' in the Ethik grade 10 topic count only if testable; an expert should judge.
grounding: ConceptBase OE-COMPETENCY-000102 (NGSS MS-LS1-2: develop and use a model)
unverified: mental models (Craik 1943; Johnson-Laird 1983) cited from memory
entries.reason: Sachsen topics use 'Modell' for trees, sector schemes, conscience theories and scale models. A stand-in built for a purpose and judged by fit covers them. Role models and untestable worldviews are left out, which an expert should check.

entries.label: Simulation

facets.AI and computation: Running a model's rules forward step by step from chosen starting values to see what follows. Changing a setting and rerunning shows how results depend on it.
facets.education: Students change settings in a simulation, such as an agent-based model, and compare outcomes with their predictions to test ideas about how a system works.

entries.curriculumUse: No Sachsen digest case tags Simulation. Typical use is classroom agent-based models and software that lets students vary settings and watch results.

entries.label: State

entries.label: Search
entries.general: Looking through a set of possible options for one that meets a goal, by trying some and checking each against a criterion.

facets.AI and computation: A program explores candidate states or answers and keeps those scoring higher on a stated objective. Web search ranks documents by a relevance score. Good-enough answers are often accepted when the best would take too long.
facets.cognition: Problem solving as moving through possible steps toward a goal, trying options and testing them. People prune the options with rules of thumb. Local search from a familiar starting point is one proposed pattern.
facets.biology: Animals search for food, mates or shelter by sampling places and moving on or staying according to what they find. Foraging theory asks which choices of where and how long to search raise food intake in a habitat.
facets.education: Learners research a question by choosing search terms, scanning results and judging sources against the question. The criterion is the learner's need, which can change as they learn.

entries.excludes: Search needs a goal and a way to check candidates. Natural selection has no goal, so calling it a search covers only the trying and keeping. Searching for meaning is a figure of speech with no candidate set. Search may stop at good enough, and the criterion can shift.

introAddition: How this space differs from the Core spaces. Bio-Core, Social-Core and Computational-Core each define their concepts inside one discipline. This space defines each concept in a general way that names what the domains share. It gives a separate meaning for each domain where a documented process or practice fits, and it says what does not carry over from one domain to another, for example whether intention is needed or whether copies exist. A concept that belongs to one discipline only, such as speciation, has no general entry. A meaning that begins with 'Technical reading' describes how computing uses a word that normally describes a mind, and it makes no claim that software has one. The added concepts and domain meanings have the status proposed. AI drafted them, a second AI checked them and no subject expert has reviewed them.
